title: Clinical Clerkship Experience at the University of Bologna, Italy
paragraphs: In spring 2025 I studied abroad at the University of Bologna in Italy and was allowed to take part in a three-month clinical clerkship.

Bologna, in northern Italy, is the capital of the Emilia-Romagna region, known for its gastronomy. When you hear Bologna you might think of "Bolognese," but the locals call it "tagliatelle al ragù," a flat, kishimen-like beef pasta. The townscape is famous for the porta, remains of the city walls, and the long arcades, and it is a quiet university town that is also a World Heritage site. The campuses and libraries of the various faculties are scattered throughout the city, as if the whole city were a university. In the center is a square with the statue of Neptune, said to be the model for the Maserati emblem, and fresh seafood, cheese, ham and vegetables can be had at the market. Everything is well supplied, from mobile phone shops, ZARA and cosmetics stores to luxury brand shops. Nearby are Venice, the city of water, Ferrara, and Modena, known for its F1 circuit and the birthplace of Ferrari. There is an international airport in the city, and the railway network is developed, so access is convenient. For Nagoya University students familiar with kishimen, the automobile industry and a convenient airport and Shinkansen network, it was a nostalgic city that somehow resembled Nagoya.

In Italy it is basically a free public system, but because of the long waiting periods, many people also use the private system. In the public system, one may wait more than a year if the urgency is low, and I saw local people several times worrying about whether to see a doctor, since they would have to wait anyway. While reaffirming the excellence of Japan's universal insurance system, I also felt points for improvement in Japan, such as the large number of tests and hospitalizations and the duplication of hospital functions. In addition, although students' clerkship hours are rather short, in the final year they must balance the thesis and the national exam, and I felt the hardship, such as going to a popular team to do odd jobs in order to write a better thesis... Also, because the department and residency program are decided only by the national exam score, the popularity of clinical departments is clear, and for example in a big city like Bologna, there is reportedly fierce competition to work in a popular department such as cardiology. I felt an institutional difference from the Japanese system of "being able to become what department you want." Looking Back Everyone I met treated me very kindly and I am full of gratitude. If one works properly in Japan, one could probably have a similar clerkship in Japanese, but meetings with people and experiences are all once-in-a-lifetime encounters, and the learning that they will never come again if missed was great. On the last day in every department, I regretted the things I had not fully understood and the times I had held back. I have a strong interest in medicine in places that are not English-speaking, and in these three months in Italy I saw far more than I had imagined and had enjoyable days meeting various people. The experience there became a great nourishment for concretely thinking about my future image as a doctor. This valuable opportunity is something I could never have obtained by my own power, and I will do my best to give back. Finally, I express my deep gratitude to Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, who gave me endless guidance and support, Dr. Itzel and all the members of the International Collaboration Office, who believed in our growth and guided us enthusiastically and kindly from our first year, the alumni seniors, and the doctors of Nagoya University who guided me on a daily basis. I also sincerely thank everyone at the University of Bologna, who graciously accepted the first-year dispatch, the people who guided me during the clerkship, the friends who supported me together, and my parents.
